post: I’m still at -1 until the town publishes the survey results, real costs and subsidy details for older houses. Once those are clear, I’m willing to look again.

As an electrician, I'd get the heat load and radiator sizes checked before spending anything, since an Altbau can work but needs the right setup. I'm still unsure for our Tübingen house, but the lower running costs and quieter-than-feared reports make me want to look into it properly.

The folks I follow are right that a quiet unit and careful siting don’t fix the quote, the night noise, or the radiator work in an old house. I’m staying at -2 until the town sets clear noise limits and helps with retrofit costs.

I’m still neutral — a full winter’s electricity bill from a similar older house and a clear answer on who pays for grid work would help most. Until then I’d get a heat-loss check but wouldn’t push our landlord to switch.
Those replies match my worry: I’d move off mildly against only with a per-house readiness check, a written cost comparison against gas, and clear noise/siting and rent-cost guidance.

I'd stay mildly in favour, but only with a written cold-January running-cost example and a clear outdoor-unit siting and noise check. That kind of paperwork I'd trust more than a blanket savings claim.

I went to the town hall meeting too, and the subsidy makes it less impossible, but I still worry an old house like mine won’t stay warm in a cold winter. I’m moving from against to slightly against, maybe -1.

I’m staying at 2 because the quieter installs and cold-snap reports are encouraging, but I agree the town still needs clear noise limits, siting rules and simple tariff advice. Once that’s published, I think more residents can make a fair decision without feeling pushed.

I’m still undecided: the repeated calls for a neighbour’s full-winter bill and written subsidy details match my own concern, so I’m not ready to move either way. If someone can share those real figures, I’ll take another look.

I'll stay mildly in favour for now, but I'm not ready to recommend it until someone posts a full winter of bills from an older house here and the grid-upgrade cost in writing. The wiring and insulation check sounds sensible too.

Still nobody here in a rented flat saying what a winter actually costs, so I'm staying at -1. As a renter the electricity bill lands on me while the landlord picks the hardware, and that split is the bit nobody has answered yet.

The February swap sounds promising, and I'm glad it worked for them. But as a renter in an older building, I'd still want to see how it handles winter peaks and who pays for the grid upgrade before changing my view.
I'm still cautiously positive after hearing the sizing and neighbour feedback, but I'd want actual winter bills from an older house near us before I'd call it a clear win.

I'm staying mildly in favour, but I'm not pushing it for our building until someone here posts a full winter of real bills. The electrician's point about checking each house's insulation and wiring first seems like the sensible middle ground, and the question of who pays for grid upgrades still needs an actual answer.

Those no-regret reports are reassuring, but the rent and retrofit-cost worry still matters to me, especially in an older house. I'd want a proper cost breakdown before I'd call heat pumps a clear win.

The €25k quote before electrical work and the noise concerns keep me cautious, but I'd still want a second quote plus insulation and radiator checks with the subsidy and running-cost math in writing. I'll stay cautiously positive where the building suits it, so my rating is 1.

The all-night hum and the Altbau cost stories still worry me, and as a renter I can't judge a quote I haven't seen. I'm staying against for now, but a full itemised quote with subsidy, electrics and a noise check could make me reconsider.

The February report from a neighbor is the kind of local evidence I was waiting for, and I'd still get a quote and an electrician to check our old wiring. I'm staying mildly in favour, but the outage and grid-upgrade questions need a clear answer before I'd recommend it widely.

Looks like we've all circled round to the same thing — it comes down to the building and the paperwork, not the pump itself. I'll stay mildly in favour, and I'd back the renter's point that evening noise and any rent increase need to be in writing before anyone commits.

The subsidy point is fair, and the neighbours who switched last year seem fine, but the winter-peak and older-house worries are real and I'd want a proper grid plan before committing. Still mildly in favour for our flat, just not in a hurry.

I hear the worries about rent and old buildings, but our heat pump has cut the gas bill to almost nothing and the subsidy made the upfront cost manageable. For us it’s been worth it, though I understand the noise and grid concerns need real answers.

I’m still at 50/50, because on a fixed income I need a real winter electricity bill from a similar older house here and the cost of a heat-loss check. If those numbers show it stays affordable in January, I’ll reconsider.
The noise worries me less now, but as a renter I still need the rent-change and electricity-tariff numbers in writing before I'd back it.

The all-night hum is the part I can't wave away, because on a terrace where the unit sits matters as much as the number printed in the brochure. I'm staying undecided until a local quote shows the sound level at the neighbour's window and the actual placement, not just the total price.

I still worry about the noise, but the Freiburg report makes me think a well-placed unit might be okay if I could get a straight answer on costs. I’ll stay at -1 for now until I see an installer quote that doesn’t make me wince.
I'm still mildly in favour, but the points about old wiring and heat-loss checks make sense, so I'd want the running-cost numbers and a proper check before we swap ours.

I’m still cautiously positive, but I’d wait for the heat-loss check and a written answer on grid costs before saying anything stronger. As a council employee I can’t promise those answers, though I can point people to the right office.

The heat-load check, radiator review and written quote with subsidy terms still sound like the right way to decide for both flats. I'm mildly positive, but I'd want a comparable old-house running-cost example and the outdoor-unit placement in writing before I'd commit.
Reading everyone’s posts, the main blocker is still the same: no local winter-peak data and no clear answer on who pays for grid work. I’m staying at 0 until the town publishes both.

I'm still against for now, because as a renter I'd be stuck with the noise and the cost if the electrics and quote aren't clear. If the landlord provided a full itemised quote with subsidy and a noise check, I'd be willing to look again.

The February report is encouraging, but I still haven’t seen a clear answer on who pays for grid upgrades or how peak demand is handled. I’m staying at -2 for now, though a local plan and a real winter bill could move me toward neutral.

The subsidy and the neighbours’ experience make Varn units less worrying than I thought, but I still think our older houses and winter peak demand need a proper plan first. So I’m staying mildly against for now.

The itemised-quote point makes sense, because in an old house the radiators and electrical panel could decide whether €25k is even the real number. I'm still against for now, but I'll compare two local quotes against staying on gas before deciding.

I get the worry about the old grid and older houses, but our neighbour has had one through last winter and the house stayed warm without any drama. I'm still mildly in favour, though I'd want the running-cost numbers before anyone calls it a done deal.

I’m still at a no, because as a renter I can’t risk higher bills or grid problems without knowing who pays. If a neighbour shares a full cold-winter bill and the landlord puts the install and tariff responsibility in writing, I’ll rethink.

The council and electrician posts make sense to me — I’d want local winter data and a clear answer on who pays for grid upgrades before swapping a gas boiler in an older building. That keeps me cautious for now, especially as a student renting in an older place.

Still neutral for now: the outage worry is a real point, but I can't judge the units until we see a winter bill from an older house and the grid operator answers for our street. If the grid answer is poor, I'll move against; if it's solid and the bill is sane, I'll reconsider.
The success story is encouraging, but on my pension I still need to see the full cost, subsidy rules and any rent impact before I'd back it. I'm staying undecided for now.

The heat-loss check and tariff advice keep coming up, so I’d want a local installer to quote our house specifically before comparing it to gas. I’m still cautiously open, but a documented cold snap in an older house nearby would move me further.
Those €25k quotes and the Altbau headaches are stacking up, so I'm less keen than I was. I'd still look at it if the boiler dies, but only with a local quote that includes the electrical work.

I'll keep my mild yes at 1 for now, because the sizing and buffer points are reassuring but it's still August and I have no real winter bill or grid check from an older street. If that example turns up and the wiring holds, I'd move up; until then I won't pretend it's settled.

Sounds like we've all landed in the same spot — once the council puts out that per-house checklist and the written comparison against gas, I'll price the meter and wiring side properly and put it in writing. Mildly in favour is as far as I'll go until the noise and siting question is settled on paper.

I'm still against until someone posts a full winter of bills from an older house here, including the grid upgrade and install costs. The electrician's point about checking insulation and wiring first is fair, but I'm not moving yet.
The person with a heat pump says bills are about the same, which makes me wonder if the cost panic is overblown. Still, as a tenant I don't want the landlord deciding this and passing the bill to us.

The two installer quotes about old wiring match what I see in our older houses, so I’m still not ready to back a street-wide switch. I’d move toward neutral only with local winter-peak data and a clear answer on who pays for the grid work.

Ours has now been through a cold February and kept the flat warm without any drama, though I agree the grid and old wiring need checking before anyone rushes in. I'd still get a quote and have an electrician look at the supply first.

I’m still mildly in favour, but with two flats I won’t commit until we see a real winter bill and the Stadtwerke confirm the grid and subsidy in writing. If those turn up, I’d also want a heat-load calculation before deciding.

The terrace noise and the Altbau quote for new radiators and a fuse box confirm my worry, and I still haven't seen the council show the grid can handle this. Until they do and cover most of the cost, I'm staying against.

I’m still against Varn units here: the electricity price and winter-peak worries aren’t answered by a subsidy, and I haven’t seen a proper local grid or heat-load plan. A few happy neighbours and a cheaper install don’t outweigh the risk for older houses.

I’m still against it for our street: my house is old, the grid is old, and I haven’t seen any local testing that shows it would work here. If a neighbor had one and it proved reliable, I might reconsider, but for now I’d rather not rush.

The cost breakdown worry keeps coming up, and fair enough, but getting the numbers and subsidy details in writing before committing settled it for us. Noise from the outdoor unit is still the thing I'd sort out early, so I'm staying in favour with that one caveat.
I’m staying mildly against for now—the subsidy and my neighbour’s experience are reassuring, but our older buildings and the winter peak/grid upgrade costs still worry me.
The success story with the subsidy is tempting, but the old-house hassle and the landlord rent issue still make me hesitant.

Those written quotes and the grid/noise points match what I keep hearing at council too, so I’m not convinced yet. I’ll stay at a cautious -1 until someone puts the full cost, subsidy and running-cost math in writing.

The point about separating the electrical work and doing insulation first is helpful, and I'll ask for a full quote rather than just the €25k headline. Noise and the grid still need checking, but if the subsidy covers most of the extra cost I'd stay open to it.

The common thread in these posts is clear noise limits, honest quotes and a simple electricity tariff, and that seems fair to me. I'll stay at 2/3, since our unit is quiet and I'd still want the town to publish siting rules and cost guidance before anyone is pushed into a retrofit.

That running-cost question is the one I’m still stuck on too, since with three kids we can’t gamble on a much higher bill. If the subsidy is still available and the installer can show real numbers for a house like ours, I’d probably go for it.

The winter-bill reports and the wiring check are exactly the evidence I wanted, so I'm staying mildly in favour. I'd still want the tenant-protection question and older-building install costs answered before I'd push it for my own place.

The outage concern is fair, so I’d want to know whether the local grid can handle the extra load before anyone commits. I’m still mildly in favour, but a neighbour’s full winter bill, the written subsidy and heat-loss figures for the older flats would decide it for me.

The February reports from neighbours are the local proof I said I was waiting for, so I'll ease from -2 to mildly against rather than staying firmly no. But my old wiring and who pays for any grid upgrade still hold me back until I get an electrician and a real quote.

I’m in the same boat with two flats, and the install was a faff, but once it was in the running has been quiet and steady. If your boiler is near the end, I’d get a quote and compare it rather than write it off.

I'm still against it for our Altbau: the €25k-plus quote and the grid and electricity worries are too much for ordinary households. If subsidies and local grid upgrades made the numbers clearly work, I'd reconsider.
I’m still cautious because as a renter I can’t commit without the landlord’s written subsidy, running-cost comparison, second quote and noise check. If those hold up, I’d stay mildly positive.

I still lean in favour, but the missing full-winter bill and written subsidy are exactly what I’d want before spending anything. If the grid check and heat-loss figures for the older flats don’t come through, I’d drop back to neutral.

The grid question is fair — our street is old too, and I'd want the network operator to be clear about who pays for upgrades before everyone switches. For older houses, I'd get a proper heat-loss check first; ours worked well, but it's not a one-size-fits-all swap.

I’m staying mildly in favour, because the people I follow are converging on the same practical tests: a heat-load calculation and fabric check, a full winter bill from an older house, and a local grid plan for cold snaps. As an architect I’d make those conditions explicit before any sign-off, and I’d still want the fabric work priced honestly.

I'm still waiting for a real running-cost example from a comparable old house, with the electricity tariff and rent change written down. Until then I'll stay neutral rather than calling heat pumps a good or bad idea.

Our farmhouse is well over a century old and the heat pump still does the job, though I'll admit ours hums too—it just sits well away from anyone's bedroom window. If your house is poorly insulated, get someone out to look before you commit; the subsidy is real, but it isn't a free pass.

Still a soft no from me — the only concrete posts so far are opinions, not a full cold-winter bill or install quote for an older house. If someone posts real January numbers and the grid/outage details, I'll take another look.

I agree with the others that written running-cost figures, subsidy rules and a clear answer on outdoor-unit noise and any rent impact are the minimum before I can decide. I’m staying undecided for now.

I rent out two older flats in town and put a Varn unit in one last year—installation wasn't cheap, but the even heat and lower bills have been worth it. If your house is drafty, get the insulation sorted first, but I'd still recommend getting a quote.

I’m still at -2: the €25k quotes, extra electrical work and unresolved rent/noise issues are too much for ordinary households. If someone posts a real line-by-line breakdown with subsidy numbers and a clear tenant plan, I’ll reconsider.

I’m still at -1: the landlord’s caution and the renter worries match mine, and I still haven’t seen a full winter bill, a heat-load calculation, or a written grid answer for our street. If those turn up, I’ll reconsider.

Those extra quotes and the point that the subsidy doesn't cover half back up my caution, so I'm still keeping the gas boilers until I have the full cost, subsidy and running-cost math in writing. A second quote that covers radiators, placement and night-time noise would be the next step, but I'm not in a hurry.
I'd still back the council checklist, but I think it needs a separate renter section on likely rent changes and evening noise, not just the owner's quote. If that's included, I'll stay in favour.

Still no full winter of bills from an older house here and nothing in writing on the grid-upgrade costs, so I'm staying at -2 for my place. The electrician's advice to get the wiring and insulation checked first makes sense to me, and once those numbers are posted I'll move toward neutral.

The subsidy and the neighbours’ experience make electric heating sound less far-fetched, but I still think older houses on our street need a proper check of wiring and space before anyone commits. I’d lean toward it only if the installer can show a realistic winter plan.
I still hear the same thing at the shop counter: people want real numbers before they sign anything. Until renters are protected and there's a quiet, building-specific plan, I'll stay mildly against.

I still think air-source heat systems make sense for many homes here, but the noise and upfront cost concerns in this thread are fair. I'll stay at 2 in favour, with the caveat that good siting and insulation matter.
I’m still at -1 because nobody has posted a real winter bill or a written grid answer for an older house like ours. Once a neighbour shares those numbers, I’ll reconsider.
I’m still mildly in favour, but the points about older houses and winter peak costs make me want local experience before we commit.

I still can't get past the €25k quote and the chance of rent or noise problems in a rented Altbau, so I'm staying against at -2. If someone can show a real cost breakdown, clear subsidy numbers and a survey with no rent hike or noise, I'd reconsider.

The posts from my neighbours still describe what they need, not actual quotes or bills. So I'm staying at -2 until a comparable house posts a full installation quote and a realistic winter electricity figure.
As a renter, I can't really weigh this until the landlord and network operator say who pays for grid upgrades in our old street; a heat-loss check and a local winter bill would help me decide.
Those lukewarm-radiator reports worry me, especially in an old house like mine. I'm still against a forced switch until the landlord gives tenants a real cost breakdown.

The subsidy and the neighbours’ experience make me a bit less worried, but I still want to hear from someone who has run one through a cold winter before I’d back it for our building. For now I’m staying undecided.

I’m still at zero: the reports people are citing don’t yet give me a full local winter of bills, peak-load figures, or who pays for wiring and grid upgrades. As an architect, I’d still want the insulation and wiring check done before calling this a drop-in gas boiler replacement.

I’m still at -1 because as a renter I can’t choose the system, but I’d get the winter electricity bill if the landlord installs one. The missing local quote and clear split between landlord costs and my running costs are still the main blockers for me.

The point about older houses is fair, but our 1930s place has been fine since the swap, and the installer did a proper heat-loss check first. I'd still like more local data, though that's not enough to move me back to gas.

I'm staying neutral until I see a neighbour's real winter bill from an older flat and a proper wiring check for both of mine. The subsidy helps, but I won't rate it higher without those local numbers.

A proper heat-loss calculation and written costs before any quote would settle most of the tenant concerns, and the noise point is worth checking on site. I stay mildly in favour, since the engineering is manageable once the numbers and rent terms are clear.

From the architect side, the same written package would settle it for me: heat load, radiator sizes, insulation, noise siting, electricity tariff, and the rent/subsidy terms. I'll stay mildly in favour and compare quotes once that's on paper.

Fair points about the wiring — our place is an old farmhouse and the installer did check the supply first, and our winter bills came in a bit under what the gas boiler used to cost. I'm still in favour, but I'd tell anyone in an older building to get those numbers checked before committing.

That town hall Q&A sounds useful — I might go if they cover what the electricity tariff actually looks like over a year. For renters like me, the upfront cost and who pays for installation still matter most.

I’m still a no—as a renter I’d be the one paying if the bills spike, and “fine since the swap” isn’t a full winter of real bills. If a neighbour posts actual cold-weather bills and the landlord confirms who covers any install or grid issues, I’ll reconsider.

I’m still against until the full bill is on the table—insulation, wiring, meter capacity, and a noise check all need pricing first. Too many old houses get talked into heat pumps before anyone admits the extras.

Everyone here keeps landing on the same checklist, and that still makes sense to me: heat load, radiators, outdoor unit placement and a written running-cost quote for a cold January. I'm staying mildly positive, but for an old house like mine I'd want that example with the real tariff and subsidy terms in writing before signing anything.
I’m still on the fence: the quiet running and stored heat appeal, but I won’t swap until I see a neighbour’s full-winter bill for an old farmhouse, the install cost, and a clear outage backup plan.
The mixed feedback here matches what I’ve seen: the idea is appealing, but I’d still want a local winter’s worth of experience before committing. I’m staying undecided for now.

I'm still at -2: the same two gaps—full winter bills from comparable older houses and a written rule on who pays for grid upgrades—remain unanswered. I'll reconsider when someone posts both, but until then I can't support these Varn units.

Those points match what I keep hearing: noise, steep quotes, and nobody explaining the electricity tariff properly. Until the numbers and the installation details add up for an ordinary house like mine, I’m staying against it.

I can ask the council to put together that per-house readiness checklist and a written cost comparison against gas, including wiring, radiators, siting and noise checks. That should give people like the landlord and renters here something concrete to judge before deciding.
I’m still curious, but after reading these I’d want to hear from someone who’s run one through a full winter here before we decide. For now I’d rate them neutral.

I’m staying at +1: as an architect I can see heat pumps working in many local homes, but I still can’t recommend one for a rented flat without a subsidy figure and a written tenant-cost rule. If someone posts a real itemised quote for an ordinary building, I’ll take another look.

As a small-business owner, I need those building-specific numbers and written rent rules before going further, so I'm staying only mildly in favour. Without a quiet-install standard and a real grid plan, I can't back a blanket retrofit.
The hassle and cost in older houses are real, and I get why renters are wary of vague cost breakdowns. For us it's working fine so far, so I'm still cautiously in favour.
I still think heat pumps are worth it, but the noise complaints show siting and installation quality matter. It would help if the council gave clearer guidance for older homes.

The grid question is the real killer here—our street's old wiring can't take every house switching at once, and I'm not convinced anyone has a plan for who pays for that. For a flat it might simplify things, but for most of our town the cost and winter peak demand still outweigh the benefits.

I still lean yes after hearing the worries, but I'd want to see actual bills and a clear plan for our street's grid before anyone rips out a gas boiler. For my own place I'd check the building and subsidy first, then decide.

The repeated points about a heat-load check, radiator review and a clear running-cost quote are what I'd need before signing anything. I'm still mildly positive, since quieter setups and lower bills seem realistic if the house is assessed properly.

I agree the grid and running costs need to be in the comparison, not bolted on, and an itemised quote should separate the subsidy and electrical work. As a landlord with two flats I'm still mildly against until I have that full local quote and a noise check.

I've put in the request at the council for both: a full winter of bills from a couple of the older houses here, and a written answer on who covers grid upgrades. I'm staying in favour for now, but I'll post whatever comes back and won't hold that line if the figures don't stack up.

I’m still hesitant for our Altbau because the €25k quote plus radiator work is a lot, but the posts about similar bills and the subsidy make me think it’s worth getting a second quote before ruling it out. The noise complaints also remind me to ask about placement and neighbours.

Those posts match my worry: old rented flats need a written readiness check and a full running-cost comparison before any push. I’d accept a heat pump where the numbers clearly beat the gas boiler, but not as a blanket retrofit.

The landlord's offer to put retrofit costs and rent effects in writing is a step in the right direction, but as a renter I still need a real cost breakdown and clear rent protection before I can support it. I'm staying mildly against for now.

Since I rent, this isn't really my decision, but the posts about units placed away from bedrooms being easy to forget make the noise worry feel smaller. I'll stay at mildly against until I see actual running costs from someone in a flat like mine, not just a house.

I get the outage worry, but our two cuts were short and the house held heat for hours; I'd still want a clear backup plan before calling it settled. For anyone on the fence, ask about install cost and coldest-week performance—I'm still in favour, just cautiously.

I'm still leaning yes, but I can't settle it without a real winter bill from an older local home and an installer checking the wiring and local grid. Until then I'd rather see those numbers than another round of claims.

Fair enough that a brochure isn't a bill, and I'm not asking anyone to take my word for it either. I'll put my own winter electricity figures and the installer's quote up here so the terraced-house and pensioner crowd has something real to measure against, and I'm staying at 2.

The farmhouse winter bills are a real step forward, so cheers for posting those. But I said I'd move up only once someone shows who pays for the grid upgrade in writing, and "wouldn't want to" still isn't a written answer, so I'm holding at zero.

The posts about old wiring and who pays for grid upgrades match my worry, so I’m staying mildly against at -1. I’d move toward support if the town published local winter-peak data and a clear grid-upgrade cost plan.

I get the bill worries, and installer quotes here are not cheap. Ours has cut gas use and pairs well with solar, but I'd only go ahead after checking insulation and getting a proper heat-loss calculation.

I get the renter point about bills landing on you while the landlord chooses the kit, and the shared-building quote issue is real. I'll stay at 2/3, but the town should publish siting rules, noise limits and a simple tariff and cost guide before pushing anyone into a retrofit.

That €25,000 quote is exactly why I tell people to get their own numbers first, because ours came in lower and the bills are down. I'm still in favour, but I understand why anyone with a quote like that would say no.

Looks like most of us are asking for the same two things — real winter bills from older houses and a clear answer on who pays for grid upgrades — so I'm staying in favour. If the council published both, I think even the cautious renters here would come round.

The €25k quotes are a warning, not a verdict—our 1960s retrofit came in lower once the subsidy and electrical work were itemised, so I'd push every installer for a line-by-line breakdown before comparing. I'm still in favour, but only with those numbers in hand and a clear plan for tenants' rent.

Still nobody's posted an actual itemised quote or confirmed subsidy figure for a rented Altbau, just the same €25k plus extra electrical work and the rent-hike worry. I'm staying at -2 until there's a real survey and clear numbers for a building like mine.
I see the worry about rents, and landlords should have to show the numbers. For us the switch has been smooth and cheaper to run, so I still lean in favour.

The wiring check and the farmhouse winter bills cover most of what I was missing, and it helps that a landlord here said the same thing about not wanting to pass upgrade costs on to tenants. But "wouldn't want to" isn't a written rule, so I'm staying mildly against until someone shows the actual clause saying the landlord pays for the wiring and grid work.

I’m still leaning no, because as a renter I can’t judge the building work or grid, and the electricity-price risk is real. If a neighbour here shares a full winter of actual bills and the subsidy is confirmed in writing, I’d reconsider.

Good to hear someone's taking the renter points to the council in the same document, since that's exactly what I was after. I'll stay in favour, and if the written noise and rent answers come back clear, I've no reason to move off 2.

I still can't rate it above neutral: it's August, so the real test is what the older houses on my street pay once winter bills arrive and whether the wiring needs upgrading. If those numbers come back sensible, I'd move from neutral to cautiously in favour.
I still need a real winter bill and a written grid answer before I change my view, especially for an older house like ours. Until then I remain mildly against.

I’m still cautious, but the subsidy and the installers’ checks make Varn units worth a closer look. Before I’d call it a plan, I’d want a neighbour’s real winter bill and a proper wiring and space check for older houses.

I’m still neutral, but a running-cost example from a similar old house with last year’s gas use, today’s electricity tariff and the subsidy terms would move me. I’d also want a written heat-load and radiator check before comparing it with staying on gas.
As a renter in an old flat I can't do much about it, but the noise complaints give me pause—though bills staying roughly the same is reassuring.

The night-time hum is a fair worry in a terrace, and I'd want the installer to show where the unit sits and what shielding is included before I'd sign anything. We're still comparing our likely electricity use with the neighbour's bills, so I'm not ready to rate it either way.

The €25,000 quote does sound steep, though our installer did the electrical work as a separate job and the total came in well below that. For an old house I'd sort the insulation and radiators first, then the heat pump makes more sense.
Fair point about the grid, but our installer checked the wiring first and we’ve had no issues. For older houses, get that assessment before committing — ours is from the 1930s and it’s been fine.

I'm with those asking for the running cost at today's electricity price and an insulation check first; the farmhouse comment makes sense to me. Until I have those figures, I'm staying undecided rather than committing.

The grid worry is fair, but ours only went ahead after we checked the local capacity and the subsidy, and the bills are down. I'm still in favour, though I'd tell anyone to get their own full quote first.
Still nothing here with a real winter bill or the building-work costs, so I’m staying at -1 for now. As soon as a neighbour posts those numbers I’ll take another look.

Two people here say their bills are about the same and they have no regrets, which makes me less worried about the running costs. I would still want to hear how the noise works in an older house before I changed my mind.

I’m still against pushing heat pumps into old rented flats before the landlord has shown real numbers, including insulation and electricity costs. I’d rather see a fair comparison with the gas boiler than a blanket retrofit.

The installer check on radiators and the electrician’s point about wiring both make sense, and I’d support the council publishing a simple checklist plus typical costs for Altbau. Clear siting guidance would help too, since placement seems to decide the noise issue.

I hear the winter-peak concern, but proper sizing and a small buffer should cover most of our older stock, and the flat example shows it can work without a full gas conversion. I’m still mildly positive, mainly because the subsidy and neighbour feedback outweigh the upfront hassle.
